opus-5.5.text:
It's a great question, and honestly it's one where the industry has been a bit sloppy, because people tend to look at a demo video and get impressed without asking what the hand actually has to do in the real world.

The way I think about it, you start with the task, not the hand. What are you picking up, how much does it weigh, how fragile is it, and how much variation is there from one instance to the next? If you're handling a cardboard box in a warehouse, you need a very different balance of strength and dexterity than if you're threading a cable or picking up an egg.

On the dexterity side, a few things matter. Degrees of freedom is the number everyone quotes, but by itself it's misleading. What really counts is how many of those degrees of freedom are independently controllable and how useful they are for the grasps you care about. Can the hand do a power grasp, a precision pinch, and in-hand manipulation, meaning repositioning an object without setting it down? That last one is the hard part, and it's where a lot of hands fall short. Sensing is also part of dexterity. A hand with good tactile feedback and accurate joint position sensing can be far more capable than a mechanically fancier hand that's essentially blind.

On strength, you look at grip force, fingertip force, and payload, but also at how long the hand can sustain that force without overheating or degrading. A hand that can hit a high peak for two seconds isn't the same as one that holds a load all shift. Backdrivability and compliance matter too. You want enough strength to do the job, but you also want the hand to give a little when it hits something unexpected, both for safety and so you don't crush what you're holding.

Then there's the tradeoff. Strength usually means bigger actuators, more weight, and more heat, and that fights against compactness and fine control. So you're always balancing. The practical test is repeatability: run the same grasp thousands of times across varied objects and measure success rate, cycle time, and failures. Durability belongs in that evaluation as well, because tendons wear, fingertips abrade, and a hand that's brilliant in the lab but needs servicing every few days won't survive deployment.

So in short, define the task envelope, measure grasp versatility and sensing as well as raw force, and then test it over and over, because reliability at scale is what really separates a good hand from a good demo.

r001.rationale: The response discusses balancing dexterity and strength, but does not clearly state that a highly dexterous hand can still be unsuitable because it lacks sufficient strength.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the first thing I'd say is that dexterity and strength are often in tension, and most of the mistakes I see people make come from treating them as a single spec. A hand that can crush a can and a hand that can pick a single screw out of a tray are usually not the same hand, so the evaluation has to start with the job, not the datasheet.

On the dexterity side, I look at three things. One is degrees of freedom, but more specifically how many of those are actuated versus passive. A lot of hands advertise twenty-plus joints, but only a handful are independently controlled, and the rest are coupled through tendons or linkages. That's not necessarily bad, underactuation can be elegant, but you need to know which it is. Two is the range of grasps it can actually form. I'll literally go through a grasp taxonomy, power grasps, precision pinches, lateral, tripod, and see how many it hits reliably, not just in a demo video. Three is in-hand manipulation. Can it reorient an object without putting it down? That's where most hands fall apart, and it's where the real value is for assembly and household tasks.

On strength, the headline number is usually grip force or payload, but I care more about where that force is available and how controllable it is. A hand might produce fifty newtons at the fingertip but only in one configuration, or it might have the force but no ability to modulate it, so it either crushes an egg or drops it. So I look at force resolution and backdrivability, and whether there's tactile sensing to close the loop. Strength without control is just a clamp.

Then there's the stuff that doesn't show up on the spec sheet but ends up deciding everything. Robustness, because fingers get hit constantly in the real world. Speed of the actuation. Thermal limits, since many hands can hit peak force for seconds, not minutes. And honestly, the quality of the software stack, because a hand you can't easily program is a hand you won't use.

So my short answer is, write down the ten objects and ten manipulations you actually need, then test against those. Benchmarks and demo reels are a starting point, not an evaluation.

r001.rationale: The response says dexterity and strength can be in tension, but does not clearly state that a highly dexterous hand may be unsuitable because it lacks sufficient strength.

astra-6.text:
I look at dexterity and strength together, in the context of the job. Can the hand pick up the objects you actually need it to handle? Can it reposition them, hold them securely, and apply force without damaging them? A hand that can do an impressive demonstration with a delicate object may not be able to handle a heavy tool, and a strong gripper may not give you the control you need for precise manipulation.

So I’d test it on representative tasks, repeatedly. Can it pick up something small, handle something awkward, and maintain its grip under load? And how reliably can it do that? The goal isn’t to have the most human-looking hand. It’s to have the right combination of dexterity, strength, and reliability for the work.

r001.rationale: It explains that a hand adept with delicate objects may fail to handle a heavy tool, showing that impressive dexterity can be inadequate without enough strength.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with the task. What does the hand actually need to pick up, how heavy is it, and how precisely does it need to manipulate it? Picking up a box is a very different problem from turning a small part inside your fingers.

For dexterity, I’d look at whether it can reliably grasp different shapes and adjust when an object shifts. For strength, it’s not just maximum grip force. Can it hold the load through the movement without slipping, overheating, or damaging the object?

And then I’d test those things together. A hand that’s strong but can’t handle variation isn’t very useful, and neither is a dexterous hand that’s too fragile for the job. What matters is how consistently it completes the actual task.

r001.rationale: It says a dexterous hand may be too fragile for the job, conveying that dexterity alone can be insufficient without adequate strength.
